claims.text: Introducing periodic multilayer interfaces into an HEA protective coating increases its resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
Multilayer interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
HEA creep can involve diffusion-controlled deformation and dislocation-controlled deformation.
Each layer in the proposed coating has a single-phase microstructure.
The HEA layers exhibit characteristic lattice distortion.
Nanoindentation creep can be used to characterize time-dependent deformation in HEAs at small length scales.
Nanoindentation creep results can differ from conventional uniaxial creep results because indentation produces multiaxial, inhomogeneous stresses.
Engineered interfaces produce local lattice distortions and lattice mismatches.
Interface-associated distortions and mismatches obstruct dislocation propagation.
Interface-associated distortions and mismatches obstruct atomic rearrangement.
The interfaces block or deflect dislocation climb across layers.
Lattice distortion associated with the multilayer interfaces reduces atomic mobility through a sluggish-diffusion effect.
The combined suppression of dislocation motion and atomic mobility increases the effective activation energy for creep.
Under identical test conditions, the multilayer coating will have a lower steady-state creep strain rate than a monolithic coating of the same composition and thickness.
Under identical test conditions, the multilayer coating will have a higher apparent activation energy for plastic deformation than the monolithic coating.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the HEA retains its single-phase microstructure without significant grain growth or phase transformation.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the multilayer interfaces remain intact and coherent.
